Newly hatched Blacktip sea catfish larvae emerge from demersal eggs measuring approximately 11 mm in diameter, a relatively large egg size for an ariid catfish that confers substantial endogenous nutritional reserves. At the moment of eclosion, the prolarvae weigh roughly 0.7 grams [Wwb = roughly 0.7 grams], a modest initial mass that reflects the considerable yolk investment allocated per offspring. This lecithotrophic stage persists for several days as the yolk-sac larva absorbs its endogenous nutrients prior to the onset of exogenous feeding. Field observations indicate that the yolk-sac larva undergoes rapid early growth, though the precise duration of the endotrophic phase remains poorly quantified for this species. The relatively high wet weight at birth compared to many marine teleosts suggests a reproductive strategy favoring larger, better-provisioned neonates capable of withstanding the energetic demands of the estuarine and coastal environments they inhabit. This initial mass also sets the stage for subsequent growth trajectories that lead to a much larger adult body size.

As individuals progress through the juvenile phase and approach sexual maturation, the onset of gonadal activity is marked by the attainment of a distinct milestone in body length. Examinations of gonad development in Blacktip sea catfish have established that puberty is reached at a total length of approximately 42 centimeters [Lp = approximately 42 centimeters], a measurement that corresponds to a substantial fraction of the species' ultimate length. The corresponding wet weight at this pubertal stage is estimated at around 695 grams [Wwp = around 695 grams], based on length-weight regressions derived from field-caught specimens across their geographic range. This substantial body mass at puberty indicates that individuals invest considerable somatic growth before diverting resources toward reproductive functions. The transition from a juvenile, non-reproductive state to a reproductively viable adult involves not only the maturation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis but also the accumulation of sufficient energy reserves to support the demands of gamete production and subsequent brood care, which is a notable aspect of ariid reproductive biology.

The ultimate body size attained by Blacktip sea catfish represents a key life-history parameter that governs maximum reproductive output and ecological interactions. Extensive sampling across the species' distribution has revealed that the maximum recorded total length reaches 85 centimeters [Li = 85 centimeters], making it one of the larger members of its genus in the Indo-West Pacific region. The corresponding asymptotic wet weight, derived from length-weight relationships, approaches approximately 5800 grams [Wwi = approximately 5800 grams], a value that reflects the substantial somatic investment required to achieve this large body size. This considerable adult mass supports a robust physiological capacity for producing large, energy-rich eggs and for engaging in the extended parental care characteristic of ariid catfishes, where males are known to orally incubate developing eggs and young. The size advantage conferred by such a large ultimate body size likely improves competitive ability in resource-limited estuarine environments and reduces vulnerability to gape-limited predators.

Reproductive output in Blacktip sea catfish is closely linked to maternal body size, with larger females exhibiting markedly higher fecundity. At the upper end of the size spectrum, a female of approximately 70 centimeters in total length can produce a maximum of 274 eggs over the course of a year [Ri = 274 eggs over the course of a year], which translates into a daily reproduction rate that is among the highest recorded for ariid catfishes when calculated over an annual cycle. This fecundity estimate was obtained from captive individuals maintained at a stable water temperature of 27.4 °C [T = 27.4 °C], a thermal regime that closely mirrors the mean annual conditions found in much of the species' tropical and subtropical habitat. The ability to produce such a large number of eggs annually is energetically demanding and is supported by the high ingestion rates exhibited by adults during the pre-spawning foraging season. This reproductive strategy, combining relatively large egg size with moderately high fecundity, positions the species as an income breeder that relies on continuous food intake to fuel gametogenesis.

Longevity in Blacktip sea catfish has been documented through both mark-recapture studies and otolith-based age estimation, providing a clear picture of its lifespan under natural conditions. The oldest individuals recorded in the wild have reached a maximum lifespan of 15 years [am = 15 years], a relatively extended duration for a teleost of this body size and metabolic rate at a temperature of 27.4 °C [T = 27.4 °C]. This estimate was derived from populations inhabiting waters with a mean annual temperature of 27.4 °C [T = 27.4 °C], a thermal regime that influences metabolic processes and growth rates throughout the life cycle. The combination of a long lifespan, moderate to large body size, and iteroparous reproductive strategy suggests a life-history pattern oriented toward the persistence of adult individuals across multiple breeding seasons. Such longevity allows for repeated reproductive events, enabling females to accumulate reproductive success over time and compensate for potential years of low recruitment. The long lifespan also implies that the species may be particularly vulnerable to overfishing, as the removal of older, larger individuals can disproportionately impact population stability and reproductive output.
